title: Reconfigurable Electric Vehicle Battery Balancing and Power Dispatch via Tropical Dynamic Programming and Pareto Dominance Filters
abstract: Electric vehicle (EV) battery management systems (BMS) utilizing reconfigurable battery systems (RBS) require deterministic, computationally tractable power dispatch across heterogeneous, aged cells to satisfy powertrain torque requests while preventing thermal runaway, localized overpotential degradation, and cell capacity divergence. Formulated as a bounded 0/1 knapsack resource allocation problem across reconfigurable submodule bypass switches, classical branch-and-bound and pseudo-polynomial dynamic programming solvers suffer from state-space explosion, severe memory overhead, and variable execution jitter that disrupt automotive embedded controllers (AUTOSAR/CAN-FD). In this paper, we establish an algebraic discrete optimization framework formulated over the max-plus tropical semiring (R_max, ⊕, ⊗) coupled with an algebraic Pareto dominance filter (Π_Pareto² = Π_Pareto) within a tropical Nemhauser-Ullmann dynamic programming architecture. Grounded in authentic electrochemical open-circuit potential models from the literature (Chen 2020 NMC-811 and Safari 2011 LFP) and evaluated on physically-parameterized battery packs spanning N ∈ {24, 48, 96, 192, 384} cells, the proposed framework is benchmarked against exact Branch-and-Cut (HiGHS), dense grid dynamic programming, and greedy heuristics under single-threaded execution. The framework achieves strict 0.00% optimality gap parity across all instances and eliminates up to 99.6% of candidate states. For distributed submodule-level controllers (N = 24 cells), TropicalParetoDP executes in 1.32 ms (7.2x faster than HiGHS and 6.0x faster than dense grid DP), comfortably satisfying the strict 10 ms CAN-FD hard real-time deadline within a fixed 64 KB static scratchpad footprint (0.0 Bytes runtime heap allocation) in compliance with ISO 26262 ASIL-D and MISRA C:2012. For centralized full packs (N ≥ 96), general-purpose MILP solvers prove faster (8.96–66.2 ms vs. 132–7105 ms), demonstrating that tropical Pareto DP is uniquely suited for distributed submodule BMS architectures rather than monolithic centralized packs.
